audit_notes: Model: classical shear-lag of a topcoat strip (modulus E_t, thickness t_t) bonded through an interlayer of areal shear stiffness k to a rigid primer, loaded at a damage edge by a line load F; xi = x/analysis_length. u'' = (k l^2/(E_t t_t)) u, E_t t_t du/dx(0) = -F, u(1) = 0 (far field). Interfacial shear tau(x) = k u(x), peak at the edge tau_max = F*sqrt(k/(E_t t_t)). Design (graded interphase, k = 2.6e10 Pa/m): shear-lag length sqrt(E_t t_t/k) = 76 um, tau_max = 50*sqrt(2.6e10/150) = 0.66 MPa. Baseline (50 um silicone-epoxy tie coat with G = 6.7 MPa, k = 1.3e11 Pa/m): transfer length 34 um, tau_max = 1.47 MPa. Expected gain ~55 %. lambda*l = 13 (design), 29 (baseline), so the far-field BC is adequate. Checks: the design k follows from an exponential modulus profile over 100 um from 1 GPa to 0.33 MPa (beta = 8), dominated by its softest ~12 um; a real sprayed gradient will be less ideal. Membrane strain in the topcoat at the edge F/(E_t t_t) = 50/150 = 0.33, i.e. large; linear elasticity is approximate at this load and the topcoat itself may tear first (tear strength of silicone ~2-5 kN/m vs a 50 N/m load: margin exists). Material limits: silicone-to-silicone cohesive strength ~1-3 MPa, so the baseline peak of 1.5 MPa is near peel initiation while 0.66 MPa is below it, which is the benefit. Caveats: the shear-lag model neglects peel (normal) stresses at the edge, which are of the same order; the reduction applies to peeling from existing damage, not to cutting. Dimensionless: lambda*l = 13 (design) and 29 (baseline); stiffness ratio 5. Simulation coefficient: shear-lag length 7.6e-5 m (informational).
